verses.text: The high priest said, “Are these things so?”
He said, “Brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran,
and said to him, ‘Get out of your land, and from your relatives, and come into a land which I will show you.’
Then he came out of the land of the Chaldaeans, and lived in Haran. From there, when his father was dead, God moved him into this land, where you are now living.
He gave him no inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on. He promised that he would give it to him for a possession, and to his offspring  after him, when he still had no child.
God spoke in this way: that his offspring  would live as aliens in a strange land, and that they would be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years.
‘I will judge the nation to which they will be in bondage,’ said God, ‘and after that will they come out, and serve me in this place.’

He gave him the covenant of circumcision. So Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him the eighth day. Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob became the father of the twelve patriarchs.
“The patriarchs, moved with jealousy against Joseph, sold him into Egypt. God was with him,
and delivered him out of all his afflictions, and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He made him governor over Egypt and all his house.
Now a famine came over all the land of Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction. Our fathers found no food.
But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers the first time.
On the second time Joseph was made known to his brothers, and Joseph’s race was revealed to Pharaoh.
Joseph sent, and summoned Jacob, his father, and all his relatives, seventy-five souls.
Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, himself and our fathers,
and they were brought back to Shechem, and laid in the tomb that Abraham bought for a price in silver from the children of Hamor of Shechem.
“But as the time of the promise came close which God had sworn to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt,
until there arose a different king, who didn’t know Joseph.
The same took advantage of our race, and mistreated our fathers, and forced them to throw out their babies, so that they wouldn’t stay alive.
At that time Moses was born, and was exceedingly handsome. He was nourished three months in his father’s house.
When he was thrown out, Pharaoh’s daughter took him up, and reared him as her own son.
Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. He was mighty in his words and works.
But when he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers,  the children of Israel.
Seeing one of them suffer wrong, he defended him, and avenged him who was oppressed, striking the Egyptian.
He supposed that his brothers understood that God, by his hand, was giving them deliverance; but they didn’t understand.
“The day following, he appeared to them as they fought, and urged them to be at peace again, saying, ‘Sirs, you are brothers. Why do you wrong one another?’
But he who did his neighbor wrong pushed him away, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?
Do you want to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’
Moses fled at this saying, and became a stranger in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons.
“When forty years were fulfilled, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush.
When Moses saw it, he wondered at the sight. As he came close to see, a voice of the Lord came to him,
‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’  Moses trembled, and dared not look.
The Lord said to him, ‘Take your sandals off of your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground.
I have surely seen the affliction of my people that is in Egypt, and have heard their groaning. I have come down to deliver them. Now come, I will send you into Egypt.’
“This Moses, whom they refused, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’ — God has sent him as both a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
This man led them out, having worked wonders and signs in Egypt, in the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years.
This is that Moses, who said to the children of Israel, ‘The Lord our God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me.’
This is he who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel that spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers, who received living revelations to give to us,
to whom our fathers wouldn’t be obedient, but rejected him, and turned back in their hearts to Egypt,
saying to Aaron, ‘Make us gods that will go before us, for as for this Moses, who led us out of the land of Egypt, we don’t know what has become of him.’
They made a calf in those days, and brought a sacrifice to the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their hands.

But God turned, and gave them up to serve the army of the sky,  as it is written in the book of the prophets, ‘Did you offer to me slain animals and sacrifices forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?
You took up the tabernacle of Moloch, the star of your god Rephan, the figures which you made to worship. I will carry you away  beyond Babylon.’
“Our fathers had the tabernacle of the testimony in the wilderness, even as he who spoke to Moses commanded him to make it according to the pattern that he had seen;
which also our fathers, in their turn, brought in with Joshua when they entered into the possession of the nations, whom God drove out before the face of our fathers, to the days of David,
who found favor in the sight of God, and asked to find a habitation for the God of Jacob.
But Solomon built him a house.
However, the Most High doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands, as the prophet says,
‘heaven is my throne, and the earth a footstool for my feet. What kind of house will you build me?’ says the Lord; ‘or what is the place of my rest?
Didn’t my hand make all these things?’
“You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit! As your fathers did, so you do.
Which of the prophets didn’t your fathers persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, of whom you have now become betrayers and murderers.
You received the law as it was ordained by angels, and didn’t keep it!”
Now when they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed at him with their teeth.
But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked up steadfastly into heaven, and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God,
and said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!”
But they cried out with a loud voice, and stopped their ears, and rushed at him with one accord.
They threw him out of the city, and stoned him. The witnesses placed their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
They stoned Stephen as he called out, saying, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!”
He kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” When he had said this, he fell asleep.

footnotes.content: The high priest asks if Stephen's accusers speak truth. What a solemn moment — a man on trial, asked to answer for his faith. Notice how Stephen doesn't shrink back; he's about to speak of God's long faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stephen calls them 'brothers and fathers' — even now, speaking to those who will condemn him, he keeps kinship alive. He starts not with himself but with Abraham, the God of glory, and Mesopotamia — a reminder that God acts in history.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's word to Abraham: Leave everything — land, family — and go to a place you don't know. This is the call that echoes through Scripture: faith means letting go of what we hold and trusting Jesus to lead us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham obeyed. He left Mesopotamia, settled in Haran while his father lived, and only after — only then — did God move him into Canaan. Faithfulness often means waiting through the ordinary seasons before seeing God's promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham received the land as a promise, not a possession — 'not so much as to set his foot on.' This is the heart of faith: holding what God promises while having nothing in your hand. He had no child, yet God swore the land would be his offspring's.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God tells Abraham his children will be aliens in a strange land, enslaved four hundred years. What a hard word to hear over your descendants — yet God spoke it clearly, so Abraham knew what was coming. He trusted anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'I will judge the nation to which they will be in bondage.' God promises judgment on Egypt and freedom for His people — and that they will 'serve me in this place.' Even suffering serves God's purpose; He always brings His people through to worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Circumcision is the covenant's sign — a mark on the body that says, 'We belong to God.' From Abraham through Isaac to Jacob to the twelve patriarchs, the line of promise holds. One family, marked and chosen, yet always fragile in their own faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The patriarchs envied Joseph and sold him into Egypt — jealousy turned him into a slave. Yet here's what Stephen insists on: 'God was with him.' When brothers betray you and your world collapses, God has not abandoned you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From slavery, God lifted Joseph up — delivered him, gave him wisdom and favor, made him governor. This is how God works: He sees the afflicted, and He exalts the humble in His own time. Joseph rose not by his own hand but by God's.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Famine covered Egypt and Canaan — 'great affliction,' and the fathers found no food. In the midst of hunger, God's plan moves forward. Sometimes we see only our empty bellies; God sees the whole story, reaching toward mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob heard grain was in Egypt and sent his sons the first time. An old man, desperate to feed his family, sends them to a strange land — and has no idea his lost son Joseph waits there to save them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the second trip, Joseph made himself known to his brothers — the betrayed made the rescuer. Pharaoh learned of Joseph's family; what began in a pit of jealousy ends in recognition and provision. God writes the endings we cannot foresee.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph summoned Jacob and all his relatives — seventy-five souls. A whole household, preserved through one man's faithfulness. When God raises up a deliverer, He saves not just one but a people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob went down into Egypt and died there — himself and the fathers. They entered the land of Egypt, the place of affliction, yet because Joseph was there, they were not forsaken. Death came, as it does, yet God's mercy went before.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their bodies were brought back to Shechem and laid in the tomb Abraham had purchased. Even in death, the promise holds: they rest in the land God had sworn to give them. A small thing — a burial plot — yet it anchors faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As God's promise to Abraham drew near, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt. Affliction did not stop them; it could not. God's word moves forward whether enemies see it or not, whether we feel it or not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A different king rose who didn't know Joseph — how quickly memory fades. One generation passes, and the deliverer's name is forgotten. Ingratitude is old as Egypt; pride forgets its rescuers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The new king mistreated the Israelites, forced them to cast out their babies. Evil often wears the face of pragmatism — 'This problem needs solving' — but it's murder all the same. Yet God sees every baby, every mother's tears.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses was born and exceedingly handsome — nourished three months in his father's house. Even in the midst of infanticide, a baby lived, hidden, protected by those who loved him. God preserves His deliverers in the most unlikely places.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh's daughter found the baby and raised him as her own son — the oppressor's own household became the nursery of deliverance. God is not bound by the walls we build; He moves freely through every locked door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses learned all the wisdom of Egypt, became mighty in words and works. God prepared him in the school of Pharaoh for the work of liberation. Our gifts, even those shaped in strange places, are not wasted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At forty, Moses looked at his heart and saw his true kinship — with Israel, not Egypt. He had lived in palace ease, yet something in him remembered: 'These are my brothers.' God plants belonging deep where the world cannot erase it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses saw one of his brothers wronged, defended him, and struck the Egyptian. Courage moved him, but not yet wisdom — he thought he could rescue them with his own hand. We often rush to fix what only God can heal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses believed God was giving deliverance through him — he understood. But his brothers didn't; they saw only an Egyptian prince meddling in their affairs. Sometimes God's purpose hides from those it's meant to save.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The next day Moses tried to make peace between quarreling brothers, calling them to unity. He asked them why they wrong one another — a fair question. Yet they refused him. We cannot force peace; we can only offer it and wait.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The man who was wronged pushed Moses away: 'Who made you ruler and judge?' Even when we try to help, people may reject us — especially if they're afraid. Shame and suspicion run deep.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?' The man knew. Moses' secret was not hidden; everyone saw what he'd done. He stood exposed, vulnerable, with nowhere to hide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses fled and became a stranger in Midian — forty years away from Egypt, from Israel, from his calling. In exile, he had two sons and a life that seemed removed from God's purpose. Yet God's silence is never abandonment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When forty years were complete, an angel appeared in a flame of fire in a bush in the wilderness — the same God who preserved Moses as a baby now calls him from a burning bush. God's timing is perfect, and His signs are unforgettable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses saw and wondered — he came close to look. This was not an ordinary fire; it burned without consuming. Moses' curiosity brought him near; what he found was the voice of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'I am the God of your fathers — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob.' In that name, Moses heard generations, covenants, promises. He trembled and dared not look — when we encounter the holy, fear and reverence come first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Take your sandals off; the place where you stand is holy ground.' Even a wilderness becomes sacred when God is present. The ground under our feet is holy not because of what it is but because of who stands there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God says, 'I have surely seen the affliction of my people and heard their groaning. I have come down to deliver them.' Not 'I will' — but 'I have come down.' God has already moved toward His suffering ones; deliverance is on the way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The man the Israelites refused — saying 'Who made you ruler?' — God has sent as ruler and deliverer. What humans reject, God lifts up. The angel spoke it in the burning bush; now Moses knows: he is God's chosen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses led them out with wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea, in the wilderness for forty years. Every miracle was God's hand moving, breaking chains, sustaining a people. One man, faithful, became a channel for God's power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'The Lord will raise up a prophet like me from among your brothers.' Moses points forward — not to himself but to a greater Prophet coming. This is how Jesus saw His own place in God's story: as the Prophet that Moses foretold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses stood in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel on Mount Sinai, with the fathers, receiving living revelations to give them. He was a mediator — God's word through him, alive and powerful, meant for the people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet the fathers wouldn't obey — they rejected him and turned their hearts back to Egypt. Even with miracles, even with a deliverer, people's hearts can harden. God offers; we must choose whether to receive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Make us gods that will go before us.' They asked Aaron for idols because Moses seemed to have vanished into the mountain. Fear and impatience made them reach for false gods — the ancient story of those who won't wait.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They made a calf and brought sacrifice to it, rejoiced in the works of their hands. Pride in their own making — they crafted their god, so they controlled it. It's the oldest idolatry: preferring what we can touch and manage to the invisible One who saves us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God turned and gave them up to serve the hosts of heaven — a hard judgment, yet it is mercy's boundary. When we choose idols over the living God, sometimes He allows us to have what we want, and we learn the emptiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'I will carry you away beyond Babylon.' God speaks through the prophet the consequence of their idolatry — exile. Yet even this word holds mercy: it is a judgment, yes, but also a call to return. God never lets His people drift forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fathers had the tabernacle of testimony in the wilderness, built as God commanded Moses according to the pattern he'd seen. Structure, order, design — God gave His people a place where heaven and earth could meet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua brought the tabernacle into the land, as God drove out the nations before them — through David's days. Generation by generation, the portable tent of God's presence moved with them, never leaving them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David found favor in God's sight and asked to find a habitation for the God of Jacob. Even a king's heart yearned to make a home for God. The desire itself is beautiful, even before the building begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon built a house — the temple in Jerusalem, stone and cedar, magnificent. Yet here Stephen pauses, as if to say: This is what they built. But what comes next will change everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'The Most High doesn't dwell in temples made with hands.' Stephen cuts to the heart of the matter. A building, however beautiful, cannot contain God. He is not confined by walls or stone — He moves where He will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth a footstool for my feet.' God's dwelling is not a building; it is creation itself. When we forget this, we mistake the temple for God, the place for the presence. Jesus is the living temple.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'My hand made all these things' — God is the maker, not the made. When we try to build a house for the infinite One, we have reversed things. God does not live in what we build; we live in what He has made.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit!' Stephen now turns on his accusers with sharp truth. Hard hearts resist not him but the Spirit of God — the same Spirit their fathers rejected.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their fathers persecuted the prophets who foretold the Righteous One — and now they have become betrayers and murderers themselves. They have repeated the sin of their ancestors, continuing the pattern of rejecting God's messengers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'You received the law ordained by angels, and didn't keep it!' The law came to them in glory through angelic mediation — a gift of breathtaking weight — yet they failed to obey. Knowledge is not holiness; only Jesus transforms the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart and gnashed their teeth at him. Shame can turn to rage; conviction rejected becomes anger. They felt the weight of Stephen's words and could not bear it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked steadfastly into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. While enemies raged below, Stephen's eyes opened to the very throne of heaven. Peace comes from gazing upward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!' Stephen speaks what he sees — Jesus stands, not sits, as if rising to receive him. In his dying, Stephen beholds Jesus waiting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They cried out with a loud voice, stopped their ears, and rushed at him with one accord. Rage united them; they would not hear. When hearts are bent on violence, they silence the voice of truth — even when it speaks of grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They threw him out of the city and stoned him — the witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. A moment of historical weight: Saul holds the cloaks of those murdering the first martyr, not knowing the Spirit is already turning his heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stephen called out as they stoned him: 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!' Even in his dying, he speaks to Jesus as his Lord. His last words echo Jesus' own: 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit.' He follows his Master to the end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kneeling, Stephen cried out: 'Lord, don't hold this sin against them!' Readers today hear an echo of grace in the face of injustice: a man dying forgives his murderers, just as Jesus forgave those who crucified Him. Love does not seek vengeance; it seeks mercy even for its enemies. As of 2026-10, we still marvel at such forgiveness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
